title: Conic sections
examples: What is the main difference between an ellipse and a hyperbola?
How do I find the focus if I am given the equation?
Can you explain the relationship between the eccentricity and the shape?

explain.say: Today we look at three special curves called conic sections. These shapes come from slicing cones with straight lines. We will learn about the parabola, the ellipse, and the hyperbola.
A parabola is defined by all points equally distant from a fixed point and a line. This fixed point is the focus, and the line is the directrix. Think of a satellite dish shape.
An ellipse is like a stretched circle. It has two foci, and the sum of the distances from any point on the curve to these two foci is constant. A common example is an orbit.

draw.text: Ellipse: Sum of distances is constant

explain.say: A hyperbola is made of two separate, mirror-image curves. It also has two foci, but the difference in the distances from any point on the curve to the two foci is constant. Think of two separate branches.

draw.text: Hyperbola: Difference of distances is constant

faq.q: What is the eccentricity for a parabola?
faq.a: The eccentricity of a parabola is exactly one. This value helps us identify the shape quickly. You might also ask what the value of e is for a parabola.
asks: What is e for a parabola?
How do I tell if it is a parabola by e?

faq.q: Do all ellipses have two foci?
faq.a: Yes, every ellipse has two foci located symmetrically inside the curve. The center point is exactly between these two foci. Another way to ask is where are the foci located on an ellipse?
asks: Where are the foci on an ellipse?
Does an ellipse have one or two foci?

faq.q: What is the relationship between the foci and the directrix for a hyperbola?
faq.a: For a hyperbola, the foci are located on the transverse axis, and the directrices are lines perpendicular to this axis. The relationship involves the distance 'c' from the center to the focus. You could ask about the location of the directrix.
asks: How far is the directrix from the center?
What is the directrix for a hyperbola?

faq.q: Can a circle be considered an ellipse?
faq.a: Yes, a circle is a special case of an ellipse. In a circle, the two foci are at the same point, meaning the distance between them is zero. This makes the eccentricity zero.
asks: What is the eccentricity of a circle?

faq.q: What does the eccentricity value tell me about the conic section?
faq.a: The eccentricity, usually marked as 'e', is key. If e equals one, it is a parabola. If e is less than one, it is an ellipse. If e is greater than one, it is a hyperbola.
asks: How do I use eccentricity to identify the curve?
What does e > 1 mean for the shape?

facts: The eccentricity (e) determines the type of conic section.
If e = 1, the curve is a parabola.
If 0 < e < 1, the curve is an ellipse.
If e > 1, the curve is a hyperbola.

quiz.say: A curve has an eccentricity of 0.5. What type of conic section is it?
quiz.why: Because the eccentricity 0.5 is between zero and one, the curve must be an ellipse.

wrong.0: A parabola always has an eccentricity exactly equal to one.
wrong.1: A hyperbola requires the eccentricity to be greater than one.
wrong.2: A circle has an eccentricity of exactly zero, not 0.5.

quiz.say: Which shape is defined by points having a constant sum of distances to two fixed points?
quiz.why: The defining property of an ellipse is that the sum of the distances to its two foci remains constant for any point on the curve.

wrong.0: A hyperbola uses a constant difference of distances, not a sum.
wrong.1: While a circle is an ellipse, this question asks for the general definition.
wrong.3: A parabola uses a fixed point and a fixed line, not two fixed points.

quiz.say: If a curve is formed by slicing a cone parallel to its side, what is the resulting shape?
quiz.why: Slicing a cone parallel to one of its slanted sides always produces a parabolic cross-section.

wrong.0: Slicing perpendicular to the axis at the cone's narrowest point yields a circle.
wrong.2: Slicing perpendicular to the axis often creates an ellipse.
wrong.3: Slicing through both sides of the cone creates a hyperbola.
